mfg1-surface-lesson-047.title: Think about the 3 Rs and circular use through the process flow
mfg1-surface-lesson-047.objective:
Distinguish reduction, reuse and recycling.
Consider environmental burdens before and after the process.
mfg1-surface-lesson-047.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 8 classifying the 3 Rs, 8 on a circular economy, and 7 creating a packaging-example record. Write the safety and quality conditions in 3 minutes.
mfg1-surface-lesson-047.summary:
Distinguish reducing generation, repeated use and returning to resources.
Check circularity benefits while preserving quality and safety.
safety: Do not mix unknown waste liquids or container contents in the name of reuse.
Do not change collection destinations or waste categories without authorization.

paragraphs.title: Distinguish three actions
paragraphs.text:
Reduce means reducing waste generation itself, reuse means using an item repeatedly after its first use, and recycle means reprocessing it as a resource. Ordering only the required amount, appropriately reusing containers and collecting by material have different purposes.
Putting something in a collection box does not by itself mean generation decreased. Separately record quantities generated and reused, collection destinations and other information.

paragraphs.title: Consider circularity from design onward
paragraphs.text:
A circular economy considers the circulation of value and resources through design, use, repair, reuse and recycling, beyond a one-way make-and-discard flow. It considers reducing waste and pollution, circulating products and materials, and regenerating nature.
Factories also consider packaging and jig life and ease of disassembly and collection. Recyclability alone does not make an unnecessary increase in use a good improvement.

paragraphs.title: Preserve quality and safety conditions
paragraphs.text:
When reusing chemical containers, check material, residues, labeling, cleaning method and approval for reuse. Mixing different liquids without authorization to increase the collected amount is not a 3 R activity.
Use the same product quantities and periods for before-and-after comparisons, and check changes in water, chemicals, energy and waste. Also examine whether saving in one place increases defects or wastewater burdens elsewhere.

paragraphs.title: Reduction and recycling proposals
paragraphs.text: Classify resizing packaging to the necessary dimensions as reduction; repeatedly using approved, suitable returnable boxes as reuse; and sending sorted offcuts to an approved collector as recycling. Record effectiveness and approval conditions separately.

terms.meaning: Reducing the generation of waste and similar outputs.
Using an item repeatedly after it has been used.
Reprocessing waste for use as a resource.
An economic approach that circulates the value of products and resources.

mfg1-surface-lesson-048.title: Organize acids, bases and salts by name and properties
mfg1-surface-lesson-048.objective:
Explain the relationship between aqueous ions and neutralization.
Do not equate the name salt with neutral or harmless.
mfg1-surface-lesson-048.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 8 on ions and neutralization, 8 on salt classification, and 7 explaining container checks. Separately summarize pH and safety in 3 minutes.
mfg1-surface-lesson-048.summary:
Acid-base strength and concentration are different.
Salt classification does not itself establish a solution's pH or safety.
safety: Do not actually mix acids and bases for learning.
Do not handle something like food merely because its name includes salt.

paragraphs.title: The scope of acid and base explanations
paragraphs.text:
This basic unit considers acids associated with hydrogen ions and bases associated with hydroxide ions in aqueous solution. Acid or base strength concerns the degree of dissociation; it is not the same as concentrated versus dilute.
Broader definitions also exist. Do not apply this aqueous explanation to every substance without qualification. A name or appearance alone does not establish that contact is safe.

paragraphs.title: Neutralization and salt formation
paragraphs.text:
In acid-base reactions, consider how hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions form water. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide can be written HCl+NaOH→NaCl+H₂O. Check atom counts and charges on both sides.
The resulting salt and liquid pH depend on the combination and quantities. Saying “neutralized” does not necessarily mean pH 7 and harmless. Adjusting an actual tank follows a separate approved procedure from analytical calculation.

paragraphs.title: Separate salt classification from solution properties
paragraphs.text:
Study salts as compounds formed by reactions involving acids and bases. Acid salts, basic salts and normal salts are classified using chemical formulas and related information; their names alone do not determine solution pH or hazards. Even a normal salt does not always give a neutral aqueous solution.
A familiar name such as sodium chloride is not evidence that other metal salts have the same safety. Check composition, concentration, the SDS and waste-liquid category.

paragraphs.title: When container names are similar
paragraphs.text: Even if both container names include salt, do not assume they can replenish the same tank. Compare product number, composition, concentration and designated process. Hold and check any mismatch. This is identification practice, not an assignment to mix chemicals.

terms.meaning: In this unit, a substance associated with hydrogen ions in aqueous solution.
In this unit, a substance associated with hydroxide ions in aqueous solution.
A phenomenon treated here as an acid-base reaction.
A compound formed through reactions involving acids and bases, among other routes.

mfg1-surface-lesson-049.title: Distinguish redox from neutralization through electron changes
mfg1-surface-lesson-049.objective:
Match oxidation and reduction to electron transfer.
Check the difference from neutralization and the reaction balance.
mfg1-surface-lesson-049.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 8 on electron transfer, 8 on two half-reactions, and 7 writing a comparison with neutralization. Check atoms and charges in 3 minutes.
mfg1-surface-lesson-049.summary:
Match oxidation and reduction through electron transfer.
Use oxidation numbers and balances to distinguish them from neutralization.
safety: Do not mix unknown liquids and metals to learn reaction equations.
Gas evolution or heat generation does not establish that a reaction is safe.

paragraphs.title: From individual definitions to the whole reaction
paragraphs.text:
Consider oxidation as losing electrons and reduction as gaining them. Electrons released by one side pass to the other, so oxidation and reduction occur together. A reaction can be redox through electron transfer even when no oxygen transfer is visible.
Earlier electroplating lessons addressed reduction of metal ions at the cathode. This unit asks a different question: follow which substance supplies electrons and which receives them across the whole reaction.

paragraphs.title: Combine two half-reactions
paragraphs.text:
In a paper example, Fe→Fe²⁺+2 e⁻ is oxidation and Cu²⁺+2 e⁻→Cu is reduction. Combining them gives Fe+Cu²⁺→Fe²⁺+Cu, with electrons canceling. Check total charge as well as atom counts on both sides.
This is a reaction-reading example. Actual reaction behavior also depends on surface films, concentrations and the environment. Do not use the equation as a reason to put metal into an unknown liquid.

paragraphs.title: Distinguish neutralization
paragraphs.text:
In H⁺+OH⁻→H₂O, the oxidation numbers of the elements considered here do not change. Do not call every acid-base reaction redox. Gas or color changes alone cannot establish the classification.
An oxidizing agent accepts electrons from the other substance and is itself reduced. A reducing agent donates electrons and is itself oxidized. Do not reverse its own change because of the impression given by its name.

paragraphs.title: Check an explanation
paragraphs.text: If a report says a metal ion released electrons to become metal, check the electron's position in the half-reaction. For a cation becoming metal, electrons are on the left: this is reduction by electron gain. Compare with a neutralization equation and explain electron transfer and oxidation-number changes separately.

terms.meaning: An equation showing electron transfer for one side's change.
A substance that oxidizes another and is itself reduced.
A substance that reduces another and is itself oxidized.
The relationship in which total charge balances on both sides of an equation.
